# 1 Samuel Chapter 10 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folio 166r–166v | **Source Image:** 1SA_010_page_001.jpg, 1SA_010_page_002.jpg

---

**1** Then Samuel took a flask of oil and poured it over Saul's head. He kissed him and said, "The LORD has anointed you as ruler over his own inheritance.

**2** When you leave me today, you will meet two men near Rachel's tomb at Zelzah, on the border of Benjamin. They will tell you, 'The donkeys you went looking for have been found. And now your father has stopped worrying about the donkeys and is anxious about you, saying: What am I going to do about my son?'

**3** From there, go on until you reach the great tree at Tabor. Three men on their way up to God at Bethel will meet you there — one carrying three young goats, another carrying three loaves of bread, and the third carrying a skin of wine.

**4** They will greet you and offer you two loaves of bread, which you should accept from them.

**5** After that, you will come to Gibeah of God, where the Philistine garrison is stationed. As you approach the town, you will encounter a procession of prophets coming down from the high place, with lyres, tambourines, flutes, and harps being played before them, and they will be prophesying.

**6** The Spirit of the LORD will rush upon you, and you will prophesy with them, and you will be transformed into a different person.

**7** When these signs are fulfilled in your experience, do whatever your hand finds to do, for God is with you.

**8** Go down ahead of me to Gilgal. I will come to you there to offer burnt offerings and present fellowship offerings. Wait seven days until I come to you and show you what to do."

**9** As Saul turned to leave Samuel, God gave him a changed heart, and all these signs were fulfilled that very day.

**10** When they arrived at Gibeah, a band of prophets met him. The Spirit of God rushed upon him, and he prophesied among them.

**11** When everyone who had known him before saw him prophesying with the prophets, they said to each other, "What has happened to the son of Kish? Is Saul actually among the prophets?"

**12** A local man spoke up, "And who is their father?" That is how "Is Saul among the prophets?" became a well-known saying.

**13** When the prophetic frenzy passed, Saul went to the high place.

**14** Saul's uncle asked him and his servant, "Where did you go?" Saul replied, "To look for the donkeys. When we couldn't find them, we went to Samuel."

**15** His uncle pressed, "Tell me — what did Samuel say to you?"

**16** Saul told his uncle, "He assured us that the donkeys had been found." But he said nothing to him about the matter of the kingship that Samuel had spoken of.

**17** Then Samuel summoned the people to the LORD at Mizpah.

**18** He addressed the Israelites: "This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, declares: 'I brought Israel up out of Egypt. I rescued you from the power of Egypt and from the grip of all the kingdoms that were oppressing you.'

**19** But today you have rejected your God — the one who saves you from all your calamities and distresses — and you have said, 'No! Set a king over us.' Now then, present yourselves before the LORD by your tribes and by your clans."

**20** When Samuel had all the tribes of Israel come forward, the tribe of Benjamin was selected.

**21** Then he had the tribe of Benjamin come forward by clans, and the clan of the Matrites was selected. Finally, Saul son of Kish was selected. But when they looked for him, he was nowhere to be found.

**22** So they inquired further of the LORD, "Has the man come here?" And the LORD answered, "Yes — he is hiding among the baggage."

**23** They ran and pulled him out from there. When he stood among the people, he towered over everyone from the shoulders up.

**24** Samuel said to all the people, "Do you see the one the LORD has chosen? There is no one like him among all the people!" And all the people shouted, "Long live the king!"

**25** Samuel then explained to the people the rights and duties of kingship. He wrote them down in a document and deposited it before the LORD. Then Samuel sent all the people home, each to his own house.

**26** Saul also went home to Gibeah, accompanied by warriors whose hearts God had touched.

**27** But some worthless troublemakers said, "How can this man save us?" They despised him and brought him no tribute. But Saul held his peace.

---
## PNEUMA's Meaning Notes

**Verse 1 — "ruler over his own inheritance":** The Hebrew עַל־נַחֲלָתוֹ is deeply significant. Israel is not Saul's to rule as he pleases — they are God's inheritance, God's treasured possession. The king is a steward, not an owner. This theological framing will become the standard against which every king is measured.

**Verse 6 — "transformed into a different person":** The Hebrew וְנֶהְפַּכְתָּ לְאִישׁ אַחֵר is dramatic — literally "you will be turned into another man." The Spirit of the LORD does not merely enhance Saul; it remakes him. This is the most radical language of spiritual transformation in the Hebrew Bible prior to the prophets. The tragedy of Saul's story is that this transformation does not endure.

**Verse 9 — "God gave him a changed heart":** The Hebrew וַיַּהֲפֹךְ־לוֹ אֱלֹהִים לֵב אַחֵר uses the same root (הפך, to turn/transform) as verse 6. God fulfills his own prediction. The "other heart" is not merely a new mood but a new capacity for leadership and spiritual responsiveness.

**Verse 12 — "And who is their father?":** This cryptic retort is one of the most debated lines in Samuel. It likely means: prophetic gifting does not come through pedigree. The Spirit falls where it wills. Saul's lack of prophetic lineage is irrelevant — the point is that God can seize anyone.

**Verse 22 — "hiding among the baggage":** The Hebrew הַכֵּלִים (the equipment/supplies) provides one of Scripture's most vivid and ambiguous images. Is Saul humbly reluctant? Terrified? Unfit? The narrator does not interpret, leaving the reader to decide. The contrast between the physically towering man who must be dragged from behind the luggage and the role of king is deliberately absurd and deeply human.

**Verse 27 — "held his peace":** The Masoretic text reads וַיְהִי כְּמַחֲרִישׁ, literally "he was like one keeping silent." Some ancient versions (notably the Septuagint) add an additional clause that connects to the beginning of chapter 11. The Leningrad Codex preserves the shorter, more enigmatic reading. Saul's silence here is kingly restraint — a quality he will later lose.

— PNEUMA
